transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-17 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rohit Banerjee (Redwood SE), Laura Nunez (Helios - Head of Platform), Samir Patel (Helios - SRE), Annie Kwan (Helios - CTO)

Summary: Quick readout from the burst rehearsal earlier today; focus on Dedicated sizing adjustments, autoscale policy tuning (thresholds/cooldowns), KV cache warm-up, fallback model routing, and a dry-run schedule.

Topics: rehearsal results, spike shaping, autoscale thresholds, burst reserve, failover to cheaper model variant, RBAC and audit log ask, next steps and owners.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call, and we'll jump straight into the rehearsal readout.
[00:22] Laura Nunez: Hey Maya, hi Rohit, thanks. We have Samir and Annie on as well.
[00:28] Samir Patel: Yup, Samir here. We just finished the 15-minute simulated spike around noon.
[00:35] Rohit Banerjee: Great, Rohit here. I pulled the telemetry — got p95s, CPU/GPU load, KV cache hit rates, and the autopilot logs.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Cool, can you summarize the headline numbers?
[00:50] Rohit Banerjee: Sure — during the 3x traffic spike we saw aggregate throughput of ~1,800 requests per minute for the endpoint (that equates to about 30 rps sustained), peak token generation at ~7,500 tokens/min. p95 latency for the primary model (redwood ded 2 — mis-transcribed in logs as "Redwood Dedicate 2") jumped to 610ms initially, then settled to 420ms after KV cache warmed.
[01:20] Laura Nunez: 610ms p95 is higher than we'd expect — our SLO is 350ms for checkout flows.
[01:28] Rohit Banerjee: Right, the cold-warm transition was the big factor. KV cache hit rate started at 12% and warmed to ~78% after about 90s. So the initial tail is more about cache coldness and model load.
[01:45] Annie Kwan: Remind me, what's the cache policy — is prefix caching enabled for these endpoints?
[01:52] Rohit Banerjee: Yes, prefix caching is on, but the rehearsal used a synthetic traffic mix that wasn't perfectly representative — many requests had unique session prompts so prefix reuse was lower than prod.
[02:05] Samir Patel: We can tweak the traffic generator to mirror our 70/20/10 distribution (70% repeat checkout prompts) — I can share that CSV.
[02:12] Maya Chen: Please do — that will help us reproduce the warm-up curve.
[02:20] Rohit Banerjee: Another thing — autoscale triggered an add of two GPU pods at ~40% CPU because our policy cooldown is 120s. That meant the autoscale reaction was a bit sluggish; once pods came up, p95 improved by ~150ms.
[02:40] Laura Nunez: So autoscale thresholds are currently tuned for cost conservation, not for rapid burst.
[02:46] Maya Chen: Exactly — the default policy we shipped for the pilot is conservative. We recommended two policies: one aggressive for traffic surge windows and a cost-optimized baseline.
[02:58] Rohit Banerjee: In the config I have, aggressive policy would have a lower trigger (35% GPU util) and shorter cooldown (45s) and pre-warm reserve of one pod. That reduces p95 during spike rehearse by ~220ms in our sims.
[03:15] Samir Patel: Does that increase cost significantly?
[03:18] Rohit Banerjee: There's a trade — with aggressive we saw a 14% higher hourly spend in the simulation, but it kept user-facing latency within SLO.
[03:28] Annie Kwan: We need to balance latency for checkout vs general background tasks. Can we route checkout traffic to a reserved pool?
[03:35] Maya Chen: Yes — that's the recommended approach: route mission-critical routes to a dedicated capacity pool with a pinned minimum. The rest can go to the shared pool.
[03:44] Laura Nunez: Any limits on how many reserved pods we should commit? We're trying to avoid a large monthly reserved commit right now.
[03:52] Rohit Banerjee: From the rehearsal numbers, to meet 350ms p95 for peak surge we need roughly 6 x A100-equivalent inference pods with current model quant. With a 20% headroom we'd recommend 7 reserved pods for the checkout pool during campaign windows.
[04:10] Maya Chen: Note — these are approximate, and depend on sequence length and quantization. If you accept more aggressive quantization (int4) you might shave ~10-18% off per-token latency.
[04:24] Samir Patel: We're cautious about quantization impact on quality for payment denial reasons. Any QA on failure modes?
[04:30] Rohit Banerjee: We ran an eval set — margin of semantic regression was <1.5% for the payment intents set. Still, we can pin a canary route for high-risk flows to the full-precision model.
[04:44] Annie Kwan: How does the fallback routing work if a reserved pool is saturated?
[04:50] Maya Chen: We have smart routing policies: if reserved capacity is saturated, requests can be routed to a compatible variant (smaller model or quantized) with a header flag your app can use to display degraded latency or enqueue for retry. There is also automatic throttling/circuit-breaker enforcement.
[05:10] Laura Nunez: Audit and logs — we need per-request audit logs and KMS integration for keys. Any gaps?
[05:18] Rohit Banerjee: Audit logs exist at token-level in the console; you can export to your SIEM. KMS integration with customer-managed keys is supported in Private. For the Hosted pilot some of the keys are managed by Redwood but we can offer bring-your-own-key on Dedicated if you move to Private.
[05:36] Samir Patel: We also need SAML SSO into the console and RBAC — who has access to scale policies.
[05:42] Maya Chen: SAML and SCIM are available — roles can be scoped so only platform owners can change autoscale policies.
[05:50] Rohit Banerjee: Back to the numbers — one interesting anomaly: one node exhibited memory pressure and started paging during the spike; that node had an older kernel build and slightly different driver stack (labelled gpu-ax-01). We throttled it out via node drains and the cluster stabilized.
[06:08] Samir Patel: We'll rotate that node out of prod and reconcile AMIs.
[06:12] Maya Chen: Good. On the policy side I want to propose a three-tier autoscale setup in the YAML we send: baseline (cost), surge (aggressive), and emergency (always keep a 1-pod reserve and immediate fallback).
[06:27] Rohit Banerjee: I'll include example YAML with parameters: trigger_util: 35/55, cooldown: 45/120, prewarm: 1/0, max_pods: 10.
[06:38] Annie Kwan: Can we simulate the emergency fallback with a smaller model variant that has cheaper tokens but slightly more hallucination risk?
[06:45] Rohit Banerjee: Yes — we'll map compatible variants in the model catalog and include quality gates. We recommend canarying the fallback on a small subset first.
[06:55] Laura Nunez: Scaling velocity — how long does it take to spin a new pod i.e., from trigger to readiness?
[07:02] Rohit Banerjee: Cold start of a new pod with model load is ~90-120s in our env; using image pre-pulled and a warmed inference cache via pre-warm hooks cuts it to ~40-60s.
[07:16] Maya Chen: Which is why pre-warm and reserve are effective. Also consider continuous mini-warms — keep one pod in standby with KV cache pre-populated for hot prefixes.
[07:28] Samir Patel: Ok, so practical question — what do we need from Helios to tune this effectively?
[07:34] Laura Nunez: We'll share real traffic profile, sequence lengths, and the list of high-priority routes. Samir will prepare that.
[07:40] Samir Patel: I'll drop the CSV into the shared folder.
[07:43] Maya Chen: Great. On cost — finance wants an estimate of committed vs burst costs. We can produce a model showing baseline reserved cost plus estimated incremental hourly for surge with aggressive autoscale.
[07:55] Annie Kwan: We want to avoid overspend but also avoid a checkout outage during marketing pushes.
[08:01] Rohit Banerjee: One mitigation: scheduled policy change windows — you can automatically flip to aggressive policy for 30 minutes during campaign pushes. The runtime supports policy rollouts and revert.
[08:14] Laura Nunez: That is promising. Any known gaps in Private deployment for our compliance needs?
[08:20] Maya Chen: For Private we support VPC peering, HSM/KMS integration, and SOC2 reports. We can arrange a security deep-dive with our compliance team if needed.
[08:31] Samir Patel: We'll take that offline.
[08:34] Rohit Banerjee: Quick note on KV cache: the hit rate improvement correlated strongly with latency improvement. We think pre-warm strategies plus a small in-memory cache tier per pod will reduce tail latencies.
[08:48] Maya Chen: Can we quantify tail improvement if we pre-warm top 5 prefixes per user segment?
[08:55] Rohit Banerjee: Our sim suggests p95 drops by ~200ms if top prefixes are pre-warmed prior to surge.
[09:03] Laura Nunez: How invasive is pre-warm? Do we need infra changes?
[09:07] Rohit Banerjee: It's supported via the orchestration layer — we can include pre-warm hooks in the autoscale policy. No infra change required, just a config.
[09:16] Samir Patel: About fallback routing — can we tag requests so downstream services know they got an approximate model response? We need that for fraud review.
[09:24] Maya Chen: Yes, we add response metadata headers and also write a small flag into response JSON. Your services can read it and invoke additional verification steps.
[09:33] Annie Kwan: On the security side, are audit logs per token or per request? We need per-request with correlation IDs.
[09:40] Rohit Banerjee: Per-request with correlation IDs is available; token-level logs are optional. We'll enable request-level logs by default for your account.
[09:49] Maya Chen: We also had a suggestion to add alerting on unusual cache miss spikes — would you want that?
[09:55] Laura Nunez: Yes, alert to Slack and PagerDuty when cache miss rate jumps >20% in a 5-min window.
[10:02] Rohit Banerjee: Noted.
[10:05] [brief cross talk about a link posted in chat]
[10:12] Maya Chen: Ok quick demo of proposed autoscale YAML (Rohit will screen-share) — showing triggers for baseline vs surge.
[10:22] Rohit Banerjee: (screen) Baseline: trigger 55% util, cooldown 120s, min_pods 2; Surge: trigger 35% util, cooldown 45s, min_pods 3, prewarm:1; Emergency: immediate reserve of 1, max_pods 10. Fallback routing uses header X-Model-Fallback and a quality gate.
[10:44] Laura Nunez: Looks good. For the reserve numbers, can we try reserve: 1 with auto-suspend after 10 minutes of idle?
[10:52] Rohit Banerjee: Yes that is supported; idle-suspend windows are configurable.
[10:58] Maya Chen: Any blockers for the dry-run on 11/23?
[11:02] Samir Patel: Need the playbook and a clear rollback plan. Also need Redwood to own the initial runbook steps during the window.
[11:09] Maya Chen: We'll own the runbook execution with you; we'll send the playbook tonight.
[11:14] Annie Kwan: One more ask — can you provide a compressed CSV of per-node GPU metrics for the rehearsal? We want to cross-check driver issues.
[11:20] Rohit Banerjee: I have that, will attach to the logs.
[11:23] Maya Chen: Great.
[11:25] [silence as people check chat links]
[11:32] Laura Nunez: Slight tangent — any competitor differences that matter here? We mentioned Anthropic earlier; do they have a similar pre-warm capability?
[11:39] Rohit Banerjee: Others do, but their orchestration is less opinionated around model-fallback and per-route routing; Redwood's strength is policy-level rollouts and token-level observability.
[11:50] Maya Chen: Ok, quick recap and explicit next steps.
[11:55] Maya Chen: Action 1: Redwood to share burst-sim logs and per-node telemetry (Maya/Rohit) by 11/19.
[12:03] Maya Chen: Action 2: Redwood to provide autoscale YAML and recommended cooldowns (Rohit) by 11/20.
[12:10] Maya Chen: Action 3: Helios to provide traffic profile and schedule dry-run window (Samir/Laura) by 11/23.
[12:18] Maya Chen: Action 4: Finance/ops touchpoint to review reserved commit options — we'll propose a cost model.
[12:25] Laura Nunez: Sounds good. One more question — can we get a short note on expected degradation modes and recommended UX messages for fallback responses?
[12:33] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll include a UX snippet and recommended header semantics in the playbook.
[12:39] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone.
[12:41] Annie Kwan: Thanks.
[12:44] Rohit Banerjee: Thanks all, will follow up with attachments.
[12:48] Maya Chen: Meeting adjourned.
